options: The current CPU percentage used by each database
A list of currently held locks only
A row-by-row log of every individual query executed on the instance
Aggregated time and count, per wait type, for every task that couldn't make progress, accumulated since the instance last restarted or the counters were last cleared
questions.explain: It's a cumulative, per-wait-type aggregate — not a per-query or per-lock log — which is why clearing it before a measurement window matters.

questions.q: What's the difference between resource wait time and signal wait time for a given wait type?
options: Resource wait time is time genuinely spent waiting for the resource itself; signal wait time is time spent ready-to-run but queued for a free CPU scheduler
Resource wait time is always larger than the total wait_time_ms
Signal wait time only applies to network waits
They are two names for the exact same measurement
questions.explain: wait_time_ms minus signal_wait_time_ms gives resource wait time; a high signal-wait share points at scheduler/CPU pressure rather than the resource itself.

questions.q: Why must you clear wait stats with DBCC SQLPERF before a measurement window?
options: Because the DMV only holds the last 60 seconds of data otherwise
Clearing is required by SQL Server licensing
Because wait stats are stored per query, not per instance
Because sys.dm_os_wait_stats accumulates since the last restart, so raw totals can be dominated by old events unrelated to the current problem
questions.explain: Without clearing, a wait type's huge cumulative total might be almost entirely from a one-time event weeks ago, making it useless for diagnosing what's happening right now.

questions.q: Why does the ranking query filter out wait types like SLEEP_TASK and LAZYWRITER_SLEEP?
options: Because they always indicate a critical outage
They're benign, always-present background waits that would crowd out the diagnostically meaningful signal if left in
Because DBCC SQLPERF automatically removes them already
Because those wait types don't actually exist in SQL Server
questions.explain: Every idle instance accumulates these background waits; excluding them keeps the top-of-list waits meaningful.

questions.q: Two servers show PAGEIOLATCH_SH as their top wait by wait_time_ms. Server A has high signal wait time on that row; Server B has almost none. What does that difference suggest?
options: Signal wait time is irrelevant to PAGEIOLATCH_SH specifically
Server B's number is impossible and indicates DMV corruption
Both servers have identical root causes with no meaningful difference
Server A likely has CPU/scheduler pressure compounding the picture, while Server B's problem is more purely the I/O subsystem itself
questions.explain: Signal wait time reflects scheduler queuing regardless of wait type, so a high signal share alongside a resource wait points at added CPU pressure on top of the resource bottleneck.
